## 1. Overview

Buses serve as a vital component of Singapore’s public transport network, connecting residential neighbourhoods, business hubs, and peripheral regions. To support the nation’s long-term mobility planning, this project conducts a comprehensive spatio-temporal analysis of commuter behaviour, moving beyond traditional mapping toward data-driven transport planning. By leveraging large-scale bus tap-on data, the study examines not only the intensity and distribution of passenger flows but also their spatial clustering and temporal dynamics.

The analysis is structured in three sections:

-   **Spatial Distribution Analysis**\
    Passenger trips are aggregated into a hexagonal Traffic Analysis Zone (TAZ) framework to build a clear spatial representation of mobility intensity during weekday morning, weekday evening, and weekend periods. This foundational layer visualises baseline travel flows and spatial distribution patterns across the island.

-   **Spatial Clustering**\
    To detect localised patterns of demand, the study applies Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA) — including *Local Moran’s I*, *Geary’s C*, and *Getis-Ord Gi\** — to identify statistically significant hotspots, coldspots, and outlier areas of bus ridership.

-   **Temporal Trend Analysis**\
    To examine how these clusters evolve, Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) integrates the Gi\* statistic with the Mann-Kendall trend test, classifying clusters as emerging, intensifying, diminishing, or sporadic over time. This captures the dynamic dimension of urban mobility.

### 1.1 Datasets

**Aspatial Data**

-   *Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Bus Stops* from [LTA DataMall](https://datamall.lta.gov.sg/content/datamall/en.html)

**Geospatial Data**

-   *Bus Stop Location* from LTA DataMall. It provides information about all the bus stops currently being serviced by buses, including the bus stop code (identifier) and location coordinates.

-   *Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea)* from [Singapore’s open data portal](https://data.gov.sg/).

## 2. Data Preparation

### 2.1 Loading the R packages

The following R packages are used:

-   

    | R Package | Description |
    |------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
    | **sf** | A package that provides [**simple features access**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_Features) for R. |
    | **spdep** | Creates spatial weights matrices and to test for and model spatial autocorrelation in geographical data, like Moran’s I and Geary’s C and Local Moran’s I and Getis-Ord G. |
    | **tidyverse** | Includes the core packages like ggplot2, dplyr, readr, purrr, tibble, lubridate, etc. |
    | **sfdep** | Builds on the great shoulders of **spdep** package for spatial dependence. sfdep creates an sf and tidyverse friendly interface to the package as well as introduces new functionality that is not present in spdep. |
    | **knitr** | Color maps designed to improve graph readability for readers with common forms of color blindness and/or color vision deficiency. |
    | **tmap** | geographical maps in which spatial data distributions are visualized. This package offers a flexible, layer-based, and easy to use approach to create thematic maps, such as choropleths and bubble maps. |
    | **rvest** | Provides the HTML parsing and extraction functions |
    | **patchwork** |  |



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, sf, spdep, sfdep, knitr,tmap, rvest, patchwork)
```
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
                  layer = "BusStop") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mpsz_sf <- mpsz_sf %>%
  mutate(
    REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mpsz_cl <- mpsz_sf %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N != "SOUTHERN GROUP",
         PLN_AREA_N != "WESTERN ISLANDS", 
         PLN_AREA_N != "NORTH-EASTERN ISLANDS")
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
write_rds(mpsz_cl, 
          "data/rds/mpsz_cl.rds")
```

##### 2.2.3.2 Extract Bus Stops within Singapore

Some bus stops are outside the polygons because of JB border and they have to be excluded**.** One way to exclude them is to plot the mpsz layer on top of the BusStop layer.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
BusStop_in_SG <- st_join(
  BusStop, mpsz_cl,
  join = st_within,
  left = FALSE)
```
:::



Plot the bus stop data again to check that the bus stops have been removed.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_cl) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(BusStop_in_SG) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.2, fill = "black", col = "grey") +
  tm_layout(main.title = "Bus Stops Within Singapore Boundaries",
            bg.color = "lightblue",
            outer.margins = c(0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Take_Home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=1152}
:::
:::



##### 2.2.3.3 Deriving Analytical Hexagon



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hexagon <- st_make_grid(mpsz_cl,
                        cellsize = 750,
                        what = "polygon",
                        square = FALSE) %>%
  st_sf()
```
:::



##### 2.2.3.4 Filtering hexagons with bus stops

To retain hexagons with bus stops. Use `st_intersects()` to return 2 values: True, False (0 or 1). The hexagon with a bus stop would be 1, and without a bus stop would return 0.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hexagon$n_collisions =
  lengths(st_intersects(
    hexagon, BusStop_in_SG))

hexagon <- filter(hexagon, n_collisions > 0)
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_cl) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(hexagon) +
  tm_fill(col = "grey20", fill = "orange", fill_alpha = 0.7) +
  tm_layout(bg.color = "lightblue",
            outer.margins = c(0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Take_Home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=1152}
:::
:::



The hexagon map shows where bus stops are found across Singapore. Each colored hexagon marks an area with at least one bus stop, making it easy to see that most bus stops are located in built-up towns and along main roads. Many other parts of Singapore, especially less developed areas, don’t have direct bus service. This map gives us a clear base to group and analyze passenger numbers later. Since the hexagons don’t have names or numbers, we’ll give each one an ID so we can keep track of them more easily.

##### 2.2.3.5 Assigning ID to each hexagon

In order to know the trips occurred in each hexagon in certain time periods, we need to give each hexagon an ID.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hexagon <- hexagon %>%
  select(,-n_collisions)

hexagon$HEX_ID <- sprintf(
  "H%04d", seq_len(nrow(hexagon))) %>%
  as.factor()

kable(head(hexagon))
```

#### 2.2.5 Create Total Trips per Hexagon dataset

*Hexagon* spatial data and *trips* aspatial data will be joined for Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA) analysis. This is to allow us to view the spatial distribution of total bus trips.

##### 2.2.5.1 Aggregate Trip Data by Hexagon

Within *trips* dataset, we calculate the total TRIPS per hexagon ("HEX_ID").



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
trips_agg <- trips %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  summarise(total_trips = sum(TRIPS, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = 'drop')

kable(head(trips_agg))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|HEX_ID | total_trips|
|:------|-----------:|

|H0002  |         173|
|H0003  |         543|

:::
:::



##### 2.2.5.2 Relational Join

Join *trips_agg* with *hexagon* on "HEX_ID".



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hexagon_trips <- hexagon %>%
  inner_join(trips_agg, by = "HEX_ID") %>%
  mutate(total_trips = replace_na(total_trips, 0))

kable(head(hexagon_trips))
```

## 3. **Spatial Distribution Analysis**

In section 2.3, we derived an analytical hexagon data of 375m to represent the traffic analysis zone (TAZ). We also processed

Time period filtering for 3 time intervals will be filtered to compute passenger trips generated by origin at hexagon level. This is also done with deriving an analytical hexagon data to represent the traffic analysis.

Weekday morning peak \>\>6am - 9am (Bus Tap Time)

Weekday afternoon peak \>\> 5pm - 8pm (Bus Tap Time)

Weekend/holiday \>\> 11am - 8pm (Bus Tap Time)

### 3.1 Peak Hour Trips by HexID

::: panel-tabset
## Weekday AM

Filter the Bus tap on the time between 6am to 9am as morning peak hours during weekdays.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
AM_weekday_sort <- trips_sort %>%
  filter(HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(6, 7, 8, 9),
         DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY") %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  summarise(AM_TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) %>%
  arrange(desc(AM_TRIPS))
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
am_plot <- ggplot(AM_weekday_sort, 
       aes(x = reorder(HEX_ID, -AM_TRIPS), y = AM_TRIPS)) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Weekday Morning Peak Hour Passenger Trips (6-9 AM)",
       subtitle = paste("Total", format(sum(AM_weekday_sort$AM_TRIPS), big.mark = ","), 
                       "trips across", nrow(AM_weekday_sort), "traffic zones"),
       x = "Hexagon ID", 
       y = "Passenger Trips") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#D0DDD0"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 6),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, color = "gray40")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)

# Display the plot
am_plot
```

### 3.2 Comparative Urban Mobility Pattern



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
AM_top10 <- AM_weekday_sort %>% slice_head(n = 10)

ggplot(AM_top10, 
       aes(x = reorder(HEX_ID, -AM_TRIPS), y = AM_TRIPS)) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Top 10 Hexagons: Weekday Morning Peak Trips (6-9 AM)",
       subtitle = "Major origin zones for morning commute",
       x = "Hexagon ID", 
       y = "Passenger Trips") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(AM_TRIPS)), 
            vjust = -0.5, size = 2.5, color = "black")
```

The chart shows the distribution of passenger trip volumes during three time periods in Singapore: weekday morning (6–9 AM), weekday evening (5–8 PM), and weekends/holidays (11 AM–8 PM). In all three periods, the curve rises steeply at the beginning and then levels off, indicating that a small number of zones account for a large share of total trips, while the majority of zones have relatively low passenger volumes. The evening period has the steepest curve, showing the highest concentration of trips in fewer zones, followed by the morning period. The weekend curve is slightly less steep, indicating a wider spread of passenger trips across zones compared to weekdays. Overall, trip volumes are not evenly distributed, with clear differences between weekday peaks and weekends.
